newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African budget may disappoint - Sanlam.
newsitem.headline: S.African budget may disappoint - Sanlam.

text.p: Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's March 12 budget was expected to reinforce fiscal discipline but could still disappoint the market, life assurance giant Sanlam said on Thursday.

Chief economist Jac Laubscher said in his budget overview that because government had publicly committed itself to a deficit of four percent of GDP in 1997/98, the market focus would not be on the figures Manuel produced, but on his policy statements on issues such as the lifting of exchange controls.

"In this regard, we believe there is a real possibility of disappointment - the market appears to discount more than the minister can possibly deliver given the constraints within which he has to operate," Laubscher said.
The low level of South Africa's foreign reserves, in particular, limited Manuel's room to manoeuvre, he said.

Although Laubscher expected Manuel to adopt an even-handed approach to exchange controls, Laubscher said there was real risk of market disappointment should the announcement not live up to expectations.
"This could result in some retracement of the recent gains in the rand exchange rate and in bond prices," he said.
Laubscher forecast budgeted government expenditure of 189 billion rand for 1997/98, a two percent decline in real terms from 1996/97.
Most of the savings would have to come from strict control over civil service wage bills through continued staff cuts and conservative wage increases.
Revenue was expected to total 163 billion rand in 1997/98, 10.5 percent up on 1996/97. This would largely come from growth in Value Added Tax and income tax receipts.
He said no major tax increases were expected.
The gross borrowing requirement was expected to be about 35 billion rand, of which three billion rand would be financed through foreign bond issues and two billion rand through treasury bills.

But about five billion could come in from privatisation, leaving about 25 billion to be raised from the local bond market, or 15 billion in new money, assuming some 10 billion rand of redeemed loans was rolled over.
"This is much lower than the 21.9 billion rand for 1996/97 and can be regarded as extremely positive for the bond market," Laubscher said.
